questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Product of Sine and Cosine
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x+2x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x-2x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{14}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7x)-\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x-x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x+x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)]}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{12}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(0-0)-\frac{1}{12}(-1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x-3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x+3x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)]}_{\pi /4}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-\frac{1}{16}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(8\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(0-1)-\frac{1}{16}(0-0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
